Case report
Anesthetic management of a patient with
stiff person syndrome
Nabil Elkassabany MD (Resident), John E. Tetzlaff MD (Director) 1,
Maged Argalious MD (Staff anesthesiologist) *
Department of General Anesthesiology and Critical Care Medicine, The Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Cleveland,
OH 44195, USA
Received 10 January 2005; accepted 28 June 2005
Abstract We describe the successful anesthetic management of a patient with stiff-person syndrome
(SPS) undergoing a right inguinal hernia repair, using a somatic paravertebral block supplemented
with conscious sedation. We also present the implications of general anesthesia in patients with SPS.
The use of regional anesthetic techniques in patients with SPS has the advantage of avoiding exposure
to muscle relaxants. The use of general anesthesia in patients with SPS carries the risk of postoperative
hypotonia due to enhancement of c-aminobutyric acid action on synaptic transmission by drugs that
have a c-aminobutyric acid agonistic action.
D 2006 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare progressive
neurological disorder characterized by muscle rigidity with
superimposed painful muscle spasms [1,2]. Muscles of the
back and upper legs are particularly affected. Widespread
autoimmune dysfunction of inhibitory mechanisms, in
particular those related to the c-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
system, has been implicated in the clinical manifestations
of SPS [3,4]. This theory is supported by the presence of
antibodies against the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) and the improvement in symptoms with the use of
benzodiazepines in this patient population. Stiff-person
syndrome may be associated with diabetes, thyroiditis, and
pernicious anemia. General anesthesia has been associated
with delayed awakening and prolonged muscular weakness
in some case reports [5]. We describe the successful
anesthetic management of a patient with SPS undergoing a
right inguinal hernia repair, using a somatic paravertebral
block supplemented with conscious sedation.
2. Case report
A 65-year-old man was scheduled for elective repair of a
large right indirect inguinal hernia. His past medical history
included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, depression, and
SPS. Past surgical history was remarkable for an uneventful

repair of a left inguinal hernia in 1965 and placement of an
intrathecal baclofen pump 9 months before this presentation.
His laboratory workup detected the presence of anti-
bodies to GAD enzyme and elevated levels of IgA and
thyroglobulin antibodies. Electromyogram findings ruled
out evidence of diffuse motor axon loss disorder. However,
there was nonspecific abnormal activation of the motor unit,
and failure of relaxation of the proximal muscle group of
both lower extremities and the right upper extremity. These
findings suggested a central disorder of the motor control
unit. Current medications included insulin, enalapril, gaba-
pentin, esomeprazole, venlafaxine, and baclofen through an
intrathecal pump. The patient was also receiving intrave-
nous immunoglobulins every 2 weeks to neutralize circu-
lating antibodies and downregulate the pro-inflammatory
cytokines [2]. He received his last dose 4 days before the
scheduled surgery date.
After discussing the risks and benefits of the different
anesthetic techniques, a right somatic paravertebral block at
T12 and L1 was selected. On arrival to the operating room,
standard ASA monitors were applied. The block was
performed in the sitting position using 5 mL of 0.5%
bupivacaine at each level. Supplemental sedation with
intravenous midazolam 1 mg, fentanyl 50 lg, and a
propofol infusion at 25 to 35 lg/kg per minute was
administered. Oxygen was supplied at 2 L/min via a nasal
cannula. Vital signs were stable throughout his surgery and
in the postoperative period. The patient reported improve-
ment of his spasticity symptoms during the procedure and
for 1 hour into the postoperative period. In the Post
Anesthesia Care Unit, he complained of nausea, which
was treated with 4 mg of intravenous ondansetron.
3. Discussion
To our knowledge, this report is the first in the literature
describing the use of a paravertebral block in patients
with SPS.
In SPS, there is antibody formation against GAD, which is
an essential enzyme in the synthesis of GABA. Loss of
inhibition from higher centers causes hyperactivity of the
peripheral motor unit and subsequent progressive muscle
rigidity and episodic spasms. Initially, the axial muscles of
the body are involved with extension to the proximal muscles
of both upper and lower extremities as the disease progresses.
The syndrome is frequently associated with other autoim-
mune disorders like thyroiditis, diabetes, and cerebellar
ataxia [1,4]. The intraoperative improvement in spasticity
symptoms in our patient is most probably related to the
intravenously administered benzodiazepine and propofol
because of their facilitation of inhibitory neurotransmission
mediated by GABA. Improvement of the spasticity symp-
toms in both the upper and lower extremities suggests a
central mechanism vs a localized effect as a result of the
somatic paravertebral block. Although the facilitatory effects
of general anesthetics (eg, propofol, midazolam, inhalation
agents) on the motor neuron in patients with SPS may
result in improvement in patient spasticity, their GABA
agonistic effect may lead to postoperative hypotonia espe-
cially with the concomitant use of muscle relaxants [5,6].
The few reports in the anesthesia literature describing the
anesthetic management of patients with SPS provide
conflicting data on the response of this patient population
to neuromuscular blocking agents. According to these
reports, the effect of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants was

prolonged in some patients [5,7] and normal in others
[8-10]. There is very little information available on the
response of adult patients with SPS to succinylcholine.
Infants with stiff-baby syndrome were found to be resistant
to the effect of succinylcholine in one report and to have a
normal response in another [11-13].
A recent report demonstrated delayed awakening and
prolonged muscle relaxation when propofol, sufentanil,
atracurium, and isoflurane were used for general anesthesia
in a patient undergoing colon resection. The authors
suggested that the prolonged muscle relaxation seen in this
patient was due to enhancement of the general anesthetic
effect via GABA action on synaptic transmission [7]. It was
also postulated that the combination of baclofen with
volatile anesthetics might lead to postoperative hypotonia
and cause prolonged muscle relaxation [6,13].
In patients with SPS receiving baclofen therapy, the use
of total intravenous anesthesia may prevent the muscle
weakness caused by the interaction between inhalational
anesthetics and baclofen [6]. We elected a paravertebral
block vs a spinal or epidural anesthetic to avoid any
potential damage to the intrathecal pump. If selected, spinal
or epidural anesthesia should be performed under fluoro-
scopic guidance to track needle entry and avoid injury to the
previously introduced intrathecal pump.
There is a theoretical advantage to schedule elective
surgery in these patients shortly after their last dose of
intravenous immunoglobulins or their last plasmaphresis
where the circulating levels of antibodies are at their
lowest [3].
4. Conclusion
Regional techniques can be used successfully in patients
with SPS. Regional anesthesia avoids exposing these
patients to the risk of postoperative hypotonia that may
result from the use of general anesthetics and neuromuscular
blocking agents.
